Dancing
dan'sing
n. and ppr. (moving the body in measured steps, chiefly in celebration; rendering Hebrew machol and karar, Greek choros)
From Old French danser, of uncertain and probably Germanic origin. Hebrew machol is a round dance, from a root meaning to whirl; the biblical picture is a circle of celebrants rather than a couple.

Biblical Definition

Scripture's dancing is almost always public, corporate, and tied to a specific deliverance. After the sea, “Miriam the prophetess… took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances” (Exodus 15:20) — women together, in response to a salvation just witnessed. When the ark came up to Jerusalem, “David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod” (2 Samuel 6:14). Two details govern that verse: it was before the LORD, and the king wore the plain linen of a priest rather than royal robes. Michal despised him for it and was judged; the dancing was not the offence, the contempt was. The Psalter commands it: “Let them praise his name in the dance” (Psalm 149:3). Ecclesiastes sets it under the seasons, “a time to mourn, and a time to dance” (Ecclesiastes 3:4), which forbids both the man who will never dance and the man who never mourns. And the parable of the prodigal makes it the sound of a father's joy: the elder brother, still in the field, “heard musick and dancing” (Luke 15:25) and would not go in. The dancing in that house is heaven's over one sinner that repenteth, and the resentful man hears it from outside.

Webster 1828 Definition

Measured motion in celebration. In Scripture it is public and corporate, tied to deliverance — Miriam after the sea, David before the ark — and it is the sound of the father's house when a lost son comes home.

expand to see more

DANCE, v.i. [Fr. danser.] Primarily, to leap or spring; hence, to leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument.

2. To leap and frisk about; to move nimbly or up and down.

3. DANCING, ppr. Leaping and stepping to the sound of the voice or of an instrument.

4. DANCING, n. The act of moving with measured steps to music; a customary expression of joy or triumph.

5. In Scripture, David danced before the ark; and the daughters of Israel went out with dances to meet Saul, 1 Sam. 18.

Key Scripture

Exodus 15:20 — "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."

2 Samuel 6:14 — "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod."

Ecclesiastes 3:4 — "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"

Luke 15:25 — "Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing."

Modern Corruption

Dancing is either forbidden outright as worldly, or imported into worship in forms Scripture never knew — private, sensual, and expressive of the self rather than of a deliverance God has wrought.

expand to see more

Two errors face each other here and both mishandle the text. Some traditions have banned dancing altogether, which requires them to be uneasy about Miriam, embarrassed by David, and silent on Psalm 149:3. That is too high a price. Others cite David to justify whatever a modern service can be induced to do, ignoring how carefully the narrative specifies the occasion — the ark of God returning to its place — and the manner, a king stripped to a linen ephod so that nothing of his rank showed. Neither the ban nor the licence reckons with what the Bible actually describes: corporate, public, joyful motion in response to a particular act of God, of which Herodias's daughter dancing for a king's pleasure (Mark 6:22) is the plain and terrible opposite.

The principle to recover is in Michal's window. She saw her husband leaping and dancing before the LORD and despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16), and the chapter ends with her barrenness. What God judged was not a failure of decorum but contempt for a man's undignified gladness over the presence of God. There is a kind of respectability that cannot bear to see joy, and Scripture is harder on it than on the excess it disapproves. The elder brother in Luke 15 is the same figure, standing in the field, listening to the music, and refusing to come in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew machol is a round dance, from chul, to whirl; karar is to whirl about, used of David. Greek choros is a band of dancers, the word in Luke 15:25.

expand to see more

Hebrew machol (H4234) — a round dance; praise his name in the dance, Psalm 149:3.

Hebrew karar (H3769) — to whirl, to dance; used of David before the ark.

Hebrew raqad (H7540) — to skip, to leap, to dance; a time to dance, Ecclesiastes 3:4.

Greek choros (G5525) — a band of dancers, a dance; the sound the elder brother heard.

Greek orcheomai (G3738) — to dance; used of the daughter of Herodias, Mark 6:22.

Usage

"Of women celebrating a deliverance: all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances (Exodus 15:20)."

"Of a king before the ark: David danced before the LORD with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14)."

"Of the sound of a father's joy: he heard musick and dancing (Luke 15:25)."
